technique: repetition with a difference — a word or shape returning changed
poem:
The handle of the barn door fits your palm
like something grown there, worn to the grain of you,
and the latch gives its two cold notes, the same
it's given every dark-mouthed morning this fall.
Your fingers know the splinter-ends, the swell
where damp has gone into the wood and stayed.
Out past the eave, the hills lie drawn and waiting,
a map you've been marking by hand all week —
the paths you walked out twice before they held,
curved line and dotted line laid down to keep.
The frost is a plain fact on the fence rail now,
and the work's half made already, there in thinking —

The quiet beds you drew are still just lines — but the ground out there is ready to start becoming them.

So — up!

The quiet beds you drew are still just lines — but the ground out there is ready to start becoming them.

So — up!
lesson: Today we work on one thing, repetition with a difference. That means a word or a whole line comes back, but something around it has changed, so the second time lands differently than the first. This poem repeats a few things. The latch gives its two cold notes the same. It names curved line and dotted line, and the big move is the full line that returns. The quiet beds you drew are still just lines, but the ground out there is ready to start becoming them. Here is why the return works. The first time you take the line in as information. The second time you already know it, so your attention shifts to what it is pushing you toward. The repeat builds pressure. By the end you want the next thing to happen. Try this. Write one line you want to matter, then say it again later word for word and change only what comes right after it. The second time through, listen for how the repeated line pushes into the last line. So up.
